newsitem.title: UK: Left-leaning UK economists await Labour call.
newsitem.headline: Left-leaning UK economists await Labour call.

text.p: Britain's top left-leaning economists, academics and thinkers were lining up on Friday for a chance to clinch one of the new plumb advisory posts likely to be offered by the new Labour government.

Labour, which routed the ruling Conservatives and won the biggest majority in its history, plans to make sweeping changes in the Treasury and Bank of England, creating a number of new senior advisory posts.
At the Treasury, it will establish a new Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) to replace the largely ignored panel of independent advisers or "wise men".

And it wants to create a new monetary policy committee at the Bank of England, where several new outside appointees will join governor Eddie George, deputy governor Howard Davies and the two executive directors already responsible for monetary policy, Mervyn King and Ian Plenderleith.
These posts are in addition to nine or so positions in the Downing Street Policy Unit, traditionally a powerhouse of ideas with a direct line to the Prime Minister.

It may mean pay cuts and maintaining a public silence -- new experiences for this well paid and generally loquacious group -- but there is no shortage of economic experts eagerly waiting the call to Blair's office.
"This is the first chance leftish economists have had to get into these positions of power for almost 20 years," said one private sector economist, previously at the Treasury.
The London School of Economics looks set be a happy hunting ground for the new government.
Labour plundered its Centre for Economic Performance (CEP) for many of its plans on unemployment and low pay and its director, Richard Layard, is tipped for a key post in the new administration.
He is mentioned in connection with the CEA, although one colleague said a part-time advisory position on unemployment and low pay might be created for him.

Hugely wealthy and a former head boy at Eton, Britain's top public school, Layard is an unlikely fit even for New Labour and his political leanings are suspect to the left of the party -- he has been close in the past to the Liberal Democrats.
Layard's CEP colleagues Charlie Bean, Paul Gregg, Alan Manning and Charles Goodhart are considered more firmly Labour and are also contenders for the party's patronage.
Bean is considered a serious macro-economist and may return to the Treasury, where he previously worked as an economist.
"He's very solid but maybe not as smooth as some of his peer group, so it depends if Labour goes for style or substance," said one former colleague.

Gregg, another unemployment expert, and Manning, a heavy-weight academic who has researched extensively on the minimum wage, are also candidates for Treasury or Downing Street posts. Failing that, they may be offered positions on the planned Low Pay Unit, which will be established to set the level of the minimum wage.
Charles Goodhart, the LSE's monetary policy man, may be summoned to the Bank of England.
But the clear front runner for a Bank position is Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs, who is thought to want to succeed George as governor.
Davies has impeccable contacts in the upper echelons of the Labour party, assisting both leader Tony Blair and finance spokesman Gordon Brown over the years.
"A place in the as yet not created monetary committee is not ideal, but he may manage to get a nod about the big job," said one former colleague.
But these academics and economic gurus are in for some stiff competition from Labour's plethora of young political advisors.
Brown's economic adviser Ed Balls, aged 30, is tipped for a senior position, possibly chairing the CEA while remaining Brown's leading aide.
David Miliband, also 30, director of policy in Blair's office, has been mentioned as a possible head of policy unit in Downing Street.
"Blair and Brown appear to like a younger crowd. The old guard could find themselves squeezed," said one LSE insider.
